To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) a dominant model is not supported by our data, but a recessive model cannot be excluded; 2) the data do not support genetic heterogeneity, but a subgroup of pedigrees with a dominant model is compatible with the data; and 3) a dominant model can be detected in a subgroup of pedigges, but the model is not supported when considering the whole sample.
the genetic model that best fits the data is the mixed model, and that the genetic model best fitting the data depends on the type of information collected in the family members.

the genetic component in breast cancer cannot be detected using the mixed model, but that the mixed model can be used to detect a genetic component in breast cancers that are only associated with breast cancer.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and use of statistical methodology for the analysis of familial aggregation of common diseases, and with the use of these methods to investigate the genetics of breast cancer.
the genetic analysis of human breast and prostate cancer.
the genetic analysis of breast cancer, a common disease with complex etiology.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a dominant gene with penetrance close to one is not sufficient to account for the familial transmission of breast and ovarian cancers in this Danish sample.
there is evidence for the existence of a genetic factor in breast cancer, but the magnitude of this effect remains to be assessed.

the segregation of a major dominant gene is compatible with the familial aggregation of breast cancer in a subgroup of the Danish population, but that the segregation of such genes is not compatible with the whole sample.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the genetic component of breast cancer is not large, but that the genetic component is not zero.
the genetic heterogeneity of the disease is a major obstacle to the identification of genes responsible for the disease.
the genetic analysis of complex diseases is a difficult task.
The main takeaway from our work is that
family studies of breast cancer should be designed to include information on environmental risk factors and to be stratified by such factors.

, for complex traits such as breast cancer, it is important to consider the interaction of genetic and environmental risk factors in the design of family studies and the analysis of the resulting data.
genetic heterogeneity, as well as geneenvironment interactions, are likely to be the major sources of complexity in the analysis of familial breast cancer.
